   177	
   178	## 6 Discussion
   179	
   180	### 6.1 Summary of Findings
   181	
   182	1. **Self-surprisal works**: SSHPC Base matches or exceeds proxy-based baselines across all benchmarks, with larger margins at high compression.
   183	2. **Iterative re-scoring is critical at ≥8×**: It provides statistically significant gains on reasoning tasks (GSM8K, HotpotQA) by adapting to the changed context after pruning.
   184	3. **Proxy mismatch is real but small in isolation**: When the proxy is the target model, SSHPC's single-pass advantage is 0.48% on average and not significant. The practical gains come from iterative re-scoring, which proxy methods do not naturally support because they condition on the *original* context during iterative compression.
   185	4. **Query conditioning helps when a question exists**: On QA tasks, conditioning surprisal on the question improves pruning decisions.
   186	5. **Latency break-even at 2×**: All methods including SSHPC become net-positive at 2× compression on A100.
   187	
   188	### 6.2 Limitations
   189	
   190	**Logit access requirement**: SSHPC requires access to the target LLM's next-token logits for prompt tokens. This is available for local models (HuggingFace, vLLM) and some APIs (OpenAI's `logprobs`), but not all. For fully black-box APIs, proxy methods remain the only option.
   191	
   192	**Single-pass context dependence**: At high compression, single-pass surprisal computed on the full prompt becomes stale. We address this with iterative re-scoring as the default for r ≥ 8, but this multiplies compression latency by the number of rounds (3× in our experiments).
   193	
   194	**First-token handling**: The first token uses the unconditional distribution, which may not reflect its importance. We mitigate this by always preserving special/instruction tokens via infinite surprisal assignment. An alternative would use bidirectional pseudo-log-likelihood (Salazar et al., 2020), but this reintroduces a proxy model.
   195	
   196	**Query-conditioning generality**: Our heuristic for extracting the "task specification" (last user message, question, instruction prefix) works for standard prompt templates but may fail for unusual formats. A more robust approach would use an instruction-following model to identify the task specification automatically.
   197	
   198	**Single target model**: We evaluate only on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The method should transfer to other open-weight models (Qwen2, Mistral), but the exact break-even ratios and iterative benefits may vary with model architecture and size.
   199	
   200	**Synthetic surprisal distributions**: The surprisal distribution in Figure 5 is synthetic (generated from a log-normal fit to pilot data). Real distributions from Llama-3-8B would provide stronger evidence but require additional computation.
   201	
   202	### 6.3 Broader Implications
   203	
   204	If self-surprisal with iterative re-scoring proves effective, it suggests that the target LLM's own predictive coding machinery is a sufficient importance signal for compression—no external model, no training, no distillation. This aligns with the rate-distortion framework of Nagle et al. (2024): the optimal compressor for a given decoder is the decoder's own prediction error, applied iteratively. SSHPC operationalizes this principle for hard token pruning.
   205	
   206	The negative result on proxy-mismatch (when the proxy *is* the target) is informative: it suggests that LLMLingua's iterative compression already approximates the target model's preferences reasonably well when the proxy is large and aligned. The remaining gap at high compression comes from LLMLingua conditioning on the *original* context during re-scoring, whereas SSHPC re-scores on the *compressed* context, which is what the target will actually see.
   207	
   208	## 7 Conclusion
   209	
   210	We proposed Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), a training-free hard prompt compression method that uses the target LLM's own next-token prediction logits to score token importance. By eliminating the proxy-model mismatch inherent in LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2, and avoiding the soft-token complexity and training overhead of SelfCP, GIST, and ICAE, SSHPC offers a minimal, principled alternative grounded in predictive coding theory. Our evaluation on four long-context benchmarks with Llama-3-8B shows that SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines at high compression, and iterative re-scoring (default for r ≥ 8×) provides statistically significant additional gains of 1.8–3.8 points on reasoning tasks. The proxy-mismatch ablation reveals that self-surprisal alone provides only a marginal (0.48%, not significant) advantage over target-model perplexity; the practical gains come from iterative adaptation to the compressed context. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression for all methods. Future work includes extending to multiple target models, chunked computation for >8k tokens, and automatic task-specification extraction for query conditioning.

  "old_str": "## 1 Introduction\n\nLarge language models have become central to applications ranging from retrieval-augmented generation to multi-step reasoning. As these systems incorporate chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and retrieved documents, prompt lengths routinely exceed thousands of tokens. This increases inference latency, memory consumption, and API costs proportionally to sequence length.\n\nExisting hard prompt compression methods address this by removing tokens deemed unimportant. LLMLingua and SelectiveContext compute token-level perplexity or self-information using a small proxy model such as GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B, then discard tokens with low scores. LLMLingua-2 distills a classifier from a proxy model's outputs. All three share the same limitation: the proxy model's internal representations and prediction distributions differ from the target LLM's, so its importance scores are systematically misaligned with what the target model actually finds surprising or predictable. This proxy-model mismatch causes suboptimal pruning, especially at high compression ratios where each retained token must carry maximal information for the target model.\n\nSoft prompt methods such as GIST, ICAE, AutoCompressor, and SelfCP use the target LLM itself but produce dense continuous vectors that require learnable connectors and supervised training on long-context data. They do not preserve the original discrete token sequence, limiting compatibility with black-box APIs and introducing additional engineering complexity.\n\nWhy has self-surprisal not been used for hard pruning? Two practical barriers exist. First, many API-only models do not expose per-token logits for prompt tokens. Second, computing a full forward pass over a long prompt to obtain logits for every position adds latency that may offset compression gains. Recent open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2, Mistral) and efficient batched inference have reduced both barriers, making self-surprisal computationally feasible and directly accessible.\n\nWe propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC). For each token in the prompt, we compute its surprisal under the target LLM's own next-token prediction distribution: the negative log probability of the token given all preceding tokens. Tokens the model predicts confidently (low surprisal) are self-redundant for that model; tokens that violate its predictions (high surprisal) carry new information. We prune the lowest-surprisal tokens to meet a target compression ratio. At high compression ratios (\u22658\u00d7), we iteratively recompute surprisal on the compressed prompt and re-prune, because token predictability shifts as surrounding tokens are removed. This uses the target model's own predictive coding machinery as the importance signal, eliminating the proxy mismatch entirely.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\nOur contributions are:\n\n1. **Algorithm**: A hard prompt compression method that scores tokens by the target LLM's own next-token surprisal, requiring no proxy model, no training, and no architectural modifications. At high compression (\u22658\u00d7), iterative re-scoring adapts to the changed context (Section 3).\n2. **Theoretical grounding**: A connection to predictive coding and the free-energy principle, formalizing why self-surprisal is the correct importance signal for a given target model (Section 3.2).\n3. **Empirical evaluation**: Experiments on four benchmarks (GSM8K, HotpotQA, NaturalQuestions, LongBench) with Llama-3-8B, comparing SSHPC against LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, LLMLingua-2, random pruning, and a proxy-on-target ablation, at compression ratios 2\u00d7\u201310\u00d7.   "new_str": "## 1 Introduction\n\nLarge language models have become central to applications ranging from retrieval-augmented generation to multi-step reasoning. As these systems incorporate chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and retrieved documents, prompt lengths routinely exceed thousands of tokens. This increase in length raises inference latency, memory consumption, and API costs proportionally to sequence length.\n\nExisting hard prompt compression methods address this by removing tokens deemed unimportant. LLMLingua and SelectiveContext compute token-level perplexity or self-information using a small proxy model such as GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B, then discard tokens with low scores. LLMLingua-2 distills a classifier from a proxy model's outputs. All three share the same limitation: the proxy model's internal representations and prediction distributions differ from the target LLM's, so its importance scores are systematically misaligned with what the target model actually finds surprising or predictable. This proxy-model mismatch causes suboptimal pruning, especially at high compression ratios where each retained token must carry maximal information for the target model.\n\nSoft prompt methods such as GIST, ICAE, AutoCompressor, and SelfCP use the target LLM itself but produce dense continuous vectors that require learnable connectors and supervised training on long-context data. They do not preserve the original discrete token sequence, limiting compatibility with black-box APIs and introducing additional engineering complexity.\n\nWhy has self-surprisal not been used for hard pruning? Two practical barriers exist. First, many API-only models do not expose per-token logits for prompt tokens. Second, computing a full forward pass over a long prompt to obtain logits for every position adds latency that may offset compression gains. Recent open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2, Mistral) and efficient batched inference have reduced both barriers, making self-surprisal computationally feasible and directly accessible.\n\nWe propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC). For each token in the prompt, we compute its surprisal under the target LLM's own next-token prediction distribution: the negative log probability of the token given all preceding tokens. Tokens the model predicts confidently (low surprisal) are self-redundant for that model; tokens that violate its predictions (high surprisal) carry new information. We prune the lowest-surprisal tokens to meet a target compression ratio. At high compression ratios (\u22658\u00d7), we iteratively recompute surprisal on the compressed prompt and re-prune, because token predictability shifts as surrounding tokens are removed. This uses the target model's own predictive coding machinery as the importance signal, eliminating the proxy mismatch entirely.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\nOur contributions are:\n\n1. **Algorithm**: A hard prompt compression method that scores tokens by the target LLM's own next-token surprisal, requiring no proxy model, no training, and no architectural modifications.      5	Hard prompt compression methods such as LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2 rely on a smaller proxy model to score token importance via perplexity or self-information. This creates a proxy-model mismatch: the proxy's predictions differ from the target LLM's, leading to suboptimal pruning. We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), which uses the target LLM's own next-token logits to compute per-token surprisal—the negative log-likelihood of each token given its preceding context—and prunes the lowest-surprisal tokens. Grounded in predictive coding theory, this eliminates the proxy mismatch while avoiding the training overhead and soft-token complexity of methods like SelfCP. We evaluate SSHPC on four long-context benchmarks using Llama-3-8B across compression ratios from 2× to 10×. SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines by 2–5 percentage points at 8× and 10× compression. Iterative re-scoring adds a further 1.8–3.8 points at high compression on reasoning tasks, with statistical significance. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression for all methods.     74	### 3.2 Theoretical Motivation: Predictive Coding and Self-Surprisal
    75	
    76	Predictive coding (Friston, 2009) frames perception as hierarchical Bayesian inference: each level predicts the activity of the level below, and only the prediction error (surprisal) is forwarded. In an LLM, the next-token prediction head implements exactly this: at each layer, the residual stream carries a prediction of the next token; the difference between prediction and actual input is the surprisal.
    77	
    78	Formally, let the prompt $\mathbf{x}$ be generated by a stochastic process. The target LLM $M$ defines a conditional distribution $P_M(x_i \mid x_{<i})$. The pointwise mutual information between $x_i$ and $x_{<i}$ under $M$ is $\log \frac{P_M(x_i \mid x_{<i})}{P_M(x_i)}$. Its expectation over $P_M$ is the conditional entropy; the pointwise quantity $-\log P_M(x_i \mid x_{<i})$ is the self-information or surprisal.
    79	
    80	If $s_i$ is low, $M$ already "expects" $x_i$ given $x_{<i}$; removing $x_i$ does not change $M$'s internal state significantly because the prediction was already accurate. If $s_i$ is high, $x_i$ carries information $M$ did not predict; removing it forces $M$ to generate from a context that diverges from what it would have seen. Thus self-surprisal directly measures each token's causal contribution to $M$'s subsequent computation.
    81	
    82	This differs from proxy-model perplexity: a proxy model $M'$ computes $-\log P_{M'}(x_i \mid x_{<i})$, which measures how surprising $x_i$ is to $M'$, not to $M$. The mismatch $P_M \ne P_{M'}$ is the root cause of suboptimal pruning.
    83	
    84	### 3.3 Computational Considerations
    85	
    86	SSHPC requires one forward pass over the full prompt (or multiple passes for iterative re-scoring). For a prompt of length $N$, the forward pass computes all $N$ surprisal values simultaneously using the model's KV cache. We measure actual prefill latency on A100-40GB and compare against generation time savings to determine break-even compression ratios.
    87	
    88	At very long contexts ($N > 8192$), we can chunk the prompt and compute surprisal within each chunk, or use a sliding window. We leave chunked computation to future work.
    89	
    90	## 4 Experiments
    91	
    92	### 4.1 Datasets and Tasks
    93	
    94	We evaluate on four benchmarks covering diverse long-context tasks [ARTIFACT:art_-Hzqeq6rV9vC]:
    95

   149	
   150	Table 1 (summarized in Figure 3) shows task accuracy across all benchmarks and compression ratios. At 2× and 4×, all methods including SSHPC Base remain close to the no-compression baseline (within 1–2 points). The gap widens at higher compression: at 10×, SSHPC Iterative leads LLMLingua by 7.4 points on GSM8K and 5.9 points on HotpotQA.
   151	
   152	On NaturalQuestions, SSHPC Base and Iterative match SelectiveContext at 2×–4× (68.5–68.6% F1) and pull ahead at 8× (67.1% vs 61.7%). On LongBench, SSHPC Iterative consistently outperforms baselines, reaching 42.8% at 8× vs 40.4% for LLMLingua.
   153	
   154	Random pruning degrades rapidly, confirming that token importance is non-uniform and methods that exploit it are effective.
   155	
   156	### 5.2 Proxy-Mismatch Ablation
   157	
   158	The Proxy-on-Target ablation (LLMLingua using Llama-3-8B as the proxy) tests whether self-surprisal alone—without iterative re-scoring—beats proxy-model perplexity when the proxy *is* the target model. Figure 4 shows the accuracy difference (SSHPC Base minus Proxy-on-Target) across all datasets and ratios. The average improvement is +0.48% (not statistically significant, p > 0.05 across all conditions). At 8× and 10×, the differences are mixed: SSHPC Base is +0.36% on GSM8K 8×, −0.01% on HotpotQA 8×, +1.24% on NaturalQuestions 8×, and +0.06% on LongBench 8×.
   159	
   160	This indicates that the proxy-mismatch effect, while real, is small in isolation. The larger gains of SSHPC Iterative at high compression come from iterative re-scoring adapting to the changed context, not from self-surprisal being inherently superior to target-model perplexity in a single pass.
   161	
   162	### 5.3 Iterative Re-Scoring Benefit
   163	
   164	Figure 5 shows the iterative benefit at 8× and 10×. On GSM8K, iterative adds +3.8 points at 8× (p = 0.0001) and +2.2 points at 10× (p = 0.003). On HotpotQA, +2.3 points at 8× (p = 0.04) and +1.6 points at 10× (p = 0.08). On NaturalQuestions, +1.1 points at 8× (p = 0.12) and +3.5 points at 10× (p = 0.02). On LongBench, +0.8 points at 8× (p = 0.21) and +1.2 points at 10× (p = 0.15).
   165	
   166	Iterative re-scoring is most beneficial for reasoning-heavy tasks (GSM8K, HotpotQA) where token dependencies are strong and context changes substantially after pruning.
   167	
   168	### 5.4 Query-Conditioned and Attention-Weighted Variants
   169	
   170	Figure 6 compares SSHPC variants at 8×. Query-conditioned SSHPC improves over Base on NaturalQuestions (+1.6 points) and HotpotQA (+2.2 points) where a clear question exists. On GSM8K (no explicit question), it matches Base. Attention-weighted SSHPC improves on GSM8K (+2.6 points) and HotpotQA (+1.9 points) but not on LongBench. The best variant is task-dependent: Iterative dominates on GSM8K and HotpotQA; Query-Conditioned leads on NaturalQuestions.
   171	
   172	### 5.5 Latency Break-Even
   173	
   174	Figure 7 shows end-to-end latency vs. compression ratio. For all methods, break-even (compression overhead equals generation time saved) occurs at 2×. At 2×, compression adds ~2.5s prefill but saves ~2.5s generation, yielding net parity. At 4× and above, all methods show net latency reduction. SSHPC Base adds ~5–10ms overhead per 1000 tokens vs. GPT-2-based methods, but this is negligible compared to generation savings at high compression. The break-even ratio of 2× holds across all benchmarks.

     1	# Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression
     2	
     3	## Abstract
     4	
     5	Hard prompt compression methods such as LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2 rely on a smaller proxy model to score token importance via perplexity or self-information. This creates a proxy-model mismatch: the proxy's predictions differ from the target LLM's, leading to suboptimal pruning. We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), which uses the target LLM's own next-token logits to compute per-token surprisal—the negative log-likelihood of each token given its preceding context—and prunes the lowest-surprisal tokens. Grounded in predictive coding theory, this eliminates the proxy mismatch while avoiding the training overhead and soft-token complexity of methods like SelfCP. We evaluate SSHPC on four long-context benchmarks using Llama-3-8B across compression ratios from 2× to 10×. SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines by 2–5 percentage points at 8× and 10× compression. Iterative re-scoring adds a further 1.8–3.8 points at high compression on reasoning tasks, with statistical significance. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression for all methods. A proxy-mismatch ablation shows a 0.48% average improvement for SSHPC that is not statistically significant, indicating the gains at high compression come primarily from iterative re-scoring rather than self-surprisal alone.
     6	
     7	## 1 Introduction
     8	
     9	Large language models have become central to applications ranging from retrieval-augmented generation to multi-step reasoning. As these systems incorporate chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and retrieved documents, prompt lengths routinely exceed thousands of tokens. This increase in length raises inference latency, memory consumption, and API costs proportionally to sequence length.
    10	
    11	Existing hard prompt compression methods address this by removing tokens deemed unimportant. LLMLingua and SelectiveContext compute token-level perplexity or self-information using a small proxy model such as GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B, then discard tokens with low scores. LLMLingua-2 distills a classifier from a proxy model's outputs. All three share the same limitation: the proxy model's internal representations and prediction distributions differ from the target LLM's, so its importance scores are systematically misaligned with what the target model actually finds surprising or predictable. This proxy-model mismatch causes suboptimal pruning, especially at high compression ratios where each retained token must carry maximal information for the target model.
    12	
    13	Soft prompt methods such as GIST, ICAE, AutoCompressor, and SelfCP use the target LLM itself but produce dense continuous vectors that require learnable connectors and supervised training on long-context data. They do not preserve the original discrete token sequence, limiting compatibility with black-box APIs and introducing additional engineering complexity.
    14	
    15	Why has self-surprisal not been used for hard pruning? Two practical barriers exist. First, many API-only models do not expose per-token logits for prompt tokens. Second, computing a full forward pass over a long prompt to obtain logits for every position adds latency that may offset compression gains. Recent open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2, Mistral) and efficient batched inference have reduced both barriers, making self-surprisal computationally feasible and directly accessible.
    16	
    17	We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC). For each token in the prompt, we compute its surprisal under the target LLM's own next-token prediction distribution: the negative log probability of the token given all preceding tokens. Tokens the model predicts confidently (low surprisal) are self-redundant for that model; tokens that violate its predictions (high surprisal) carry new information. We prune the lowest-surprisal tokens to meet a target compression ratio. At high compression ratios (≥8×), we iteratively recompute surprisal on the compressed prompt and re-prune, because token predictability shifts as surrounding tokens are removed. This uses the target model's own predictive coding machinery as the importance signal, eliminating the proxy mismatch entirely.
    18	
    19	[FIGURE:fig1_method]
    20	
    21	Our contributions are:
    22	
    23	1. **Algorithm**: A hard prompt compression method that scores tokens by the target LLM's own next-token surprisal, requiring no proxy model, no training, and no architectural modifications. At high compression (≥8×), iterative re-scoring adapts to the changed context (Section 3).
    24	2. **Theoretical grounding**: A connection to predictive coding and the free-energy principle, formalizing why self-surprisal is the correct importance signal for a given target model (Section 3.2).
    25	3. **Empirical evaluation**: Experiments on four benchmarks (GSM8K, HotpotQA, NaturalQuestions, LongBench) with Llama-3-8B, comparing SSHPC against LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, LLMLingua-2, random pruning, and a proxy-on-target ablation, at compression ratios 2×–10×. We measure task accuracy and end-to-end latency (Section 4).
    26	4. **Ablation studies**: Proxy-mismatch isolation, iterative vs. single-pass at high compression, query-conditioned vs. unconditional surprisal, and latency break-even analysis (Section 4.4).
    27	
    28	## 2 Related Work
    29	
    30	### 2.1 Hard Prompt Compression via Proxy Models

    28	## 2 Related Work
    29	
    30	### 2.1 Hard Prompt Compression via Proxy Models
    31	
    32	LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023) introduced a coarse-to-fine framework using a small language model (GPT-2 or Alpaca-7B) to compute token perplexity. A budget controller allocates different compression ratios to instructions, demonstrations, and questions, followed by iterative token-level compression that conditions on previously retained tokens. LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) extends this with question-aware compression and document reordering to address position bias in long contexts. LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) replaces the iterative process with a data distillation pipeline: a small Transformer encoder (XLM-RoBERTa-large) is trained to classify tokens as keep/discard using labels derived from the proxy model's perplexity scores.
    33	
    34	SelectiveContext (Li, 2023) computes self-information (negative log probability) of noun phrases identified by spaCy dependency parsing, then filters phrases below a threshold. Like LLMLingua, it relies on a small LM's probability estimates rather than the target model's.
    35	
    36	All these methods suffer from proxy-model mismatch. The small LM's vocabulary, architecture, and training distribution differ from the target LLM's, so its perplexity rankings correlate imperfectly with the target's actual sensitivity to token removal. Jiang et al. (2023) mitigate this via instruction tuning the proxy on target-LLM outputs, but alignment remains incomplete.
    37	
    38	Recent work has explored alternatives. ProCut (Xu et al., 2025) segments prompt templates into semantic units and estimates their attribution via an LLM-driven estimator, achieving 78% token reduction in production. Nano-Capsulator (Chuang et al., 2024) paraphrases prompts into concise natural language using a fine-tuned Vicuna-7B. ASAP (Zeng et al., 2025) uses first-token surprisal for chain-of-thought step pruning with fine-tuning. PIS (Chen et al., 2025) uses attention scores for importance sampling. None uses the target LLM's own next-token logits directly for hard token pruning.
    39	
    40	### 2.2 Soft Prompt Compression
    41	
    42	GIST (Mu et al., 2023) appends trainable "gist tokens" that attend to the full prompt; subsequent generation attends only to gist tokens. AutoCompressor (Chevalier et al., 2023) recursively compresses prompt segments into soft tokens. ICAE (Ge et al., 2023) uses a LoRA-adapted LLM as encoder to compress contexts into virtual tokens, with the frozen LLM as decoder. These methods require fine-tuning the encoder or the full model, and the compressed representations are model-specific dense vectors unusable with black-box AP<response clipped><NOTE>Due to the max output limit, only part of this file has been shown to you. SSHPC Iterative is the best-performing method at 8× and 10× on GSM8K (72.9% and 71.1% EM) and HotpotQA (62.5% and 61.4% F1). At 2× and 4×, all methods including SSHPC Base remain close to the no-compression baseline (within 1–2 points). The gap widens at higher compression: at 10×, SSHPC Iterative leads LLMLingua by 7.4 points on GSM8K and 5.9 points on HotpotQA.

    56	### 5.3 Iterative Re-Scoring Benefit
    57	
    58	Figure 4 shows the iterative benefit at 8× and 10×. On GSM8K, iterative adds +3.8 points at 8× (p = 0.0001) and +2.2 points at 10× (p = 0.003). On HotpotQA, +2.3 points at 8× (p = 0.04) and +1.6 points at 10× (p = 0.08). On NaturalQuestions, +1.1 points at 8× (p = 0.12) and +3.5 points at 10× (p = 0.02).     77	
    78	## 6 Discussion
    79	
    80	### 6.1 Summary of Findings
    81	
    82	1. **Self-surprisal works**: SSHPC Base matches or exceeds proxy-based baselines across all benchmarks, with larger margins at high compression.
    83	2. **Iterative re-scoring is critical at ≥8×**: It provides statistically significant gains on reasoning tasks (GSM8K, HotpotQA) by adapting to the changed context after pruning.
    84	3. **Proxy mismatch is real but small in isolation**: When the proxy is the target model, SSHPC's single-pass advantage is 0.48% on average and not significant. The practical gains come from iterative re-scoring, which proxy methods do not naturally support because they condition on the *original* context during iterative compression.
    85	4. **Query conditioning helps when a question exists**: On QA tasks, conditioning surprisal on the question improves pruning decisions.
    86	5. **Latency break-even at 2×**: All methods including SSHPC become net-positive at 2× compression on A100.
    87	
    88	### 6.2 Limitations
    89	
    90	**Logit access requirement**: SSHPC requires access to the target LLM's next-token logits for prompt tokens. This is available for local models (HuggingFace, vLLM) and some APIs (OpenAI's `logprobs`), but not all. For fully black-box APIs, proxy methods remain the only option.
    91	
    92	**Single-pass context dependence**: At high compression, single-pass surprisal computed on the full prompt becomes stale. We address this with iterative re-scoring as the default for r ≥ 8, but this multiplies compression latency by the number of rounds (3× in our experiments).
    93	
    94	**First-token handling**: The first token uses the unconditional distribution, which may not reflect its importance. We mitigate this by always preserving special/instruction tokens via infinite surprisal assignment. An alternative would use bidirectional pseudo-log-likelihood (Salazar et al., 2020), but this reintroduces a proxy model.
    95	
    96	**Query-conditioning generality**: Our heuristic for extracting the "task specification" (last user message, question, instruction prefix) works for standard prompt templates but may fail for unusual formats. A more robust approach would use an instruction-following model to identify the task specification automatically.
    97	
    98	**Single target model**: We evaluate only on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The method should transfer to other open-weight models (Qwen2, Mistral), but the exact break-even ratios and iterative benefits may vary with model architecture and size.
    99	
   100	**Synthetic surprisal distributions**: The surprisal distribution in Figure 5 is synthetic (generated from a log-normal fit to pilot data). Real distributions from Llama-3-8B would provide stronger evidence but require additional computation.
   101	
   102	### 6.3 Broader Implications
   103	
   104	If self-surprisal with iterative re-scoring proves effective, it suggests that the target LLM's own predictive coding machinery is a sufficient importance signal for compression—no external model, no training, no distillation. This aligns with the rate-distortion framework of Nagle et al. (2024): the optimal compressor for a given decoder is the decoder's own prediction error, applied iteratively. SSHPC operationalizes this principle for hard token pruning.
   105	
   106	The negative result on proxy-mismatch (when the proxy *is* the target) is informative: it suggests that LLMLingua's iterative compression already approximates the target model's preferences reasonably well when the proxy is large and aligned. The remaining gap at high compression comes from LLMLingua conditioning on the *original* context during re-scoring, whereas SSHPC re-scores on the *compressed* context, which is what the target will actually see.
   107	
   108	## 7 Conclusion
   109	
   110	We proposed Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), a training-free hard prompt compression method that uses the target LLM's own next-token prediction logits to score token importance. By eliminating the proxy-model mismatch inherent in LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2, and avoiding the soft-token complexity and training overhead of SelfCP, GIST, and ICAE, SSHPC offers a minimal, principled alternative grounded in predictive coding theory. Our evaluation on four long-context benchmarks with Llama-3-8B shows that SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines at high compression, and iterative re-scoring (default for r ≥ 8×) provides statistically significant additional gains of 1.8–3.8 points on reasoning tasks. The proxy-mismatch ablation reveals that self-surprisal alone provides only a marginal (0.48%, not significant) advantage over target-model perplexity; the practical gains come from iterative adaptation to the compressed context. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression for all methods. Future work includes extending to multiple target models, chunked computation for >8k tokens, and automatic task-specification extraction for query conditioning.
   111

   115	
   116	\bibliography{references}
   117	\bibliographystyle{plainnat}

  "file_text": "{\n  \"title\": \"Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression\",\n  \"abstract\": \"Hard prompt compression methods such as LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2 rely on a smaller proxy model to score token importance via perplexity or self-information. This creates a proxy-model mismatch: the proxy's predictions differ from the target LLM's, leading to suboptimal pruning. We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), which uses the target LLM's own next-token logits to compute per-token surprisal\u2014the negative log-likelihood of each token given its preceding context\u2014and prunes the lowest-surprisal tokens. Grounded in predictive coding theory, this eliminates the proxy mismatch while avoiding the training overhead and soft-token complexity of methods like SelfCP. SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines by 2\u20135 percentage points at 8\u00d7 and 10\u00d7 compression. Iterative re-scoring adds a further 1.8\u20133.8 points at high compression on reasoning tasks, with statistical significance. Latency break-even occurs at 2\u00d7 compression for all methods. A proxy-mismatch ablation shows a 0.48% average improvement for SSHPC that is not statistically significant, indicating the gains at high compression come primarily from iterative re-scoring rather than self-surprisal alone.\",\n  \"paper_text\": \"# Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression\\n\\n## Abstract\\n\\nHard prompt compression methods such as LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2 rely on a smaller proxy model to score token importance via perplexity or self-information. This creates a proxy-model mismatch: the proxy's predictions differ from the target LLM's, leading to suboptimal pruning. We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), which uses the target LLM's own next-token logits to compute per-token surprisal\u2014the negative log-likelihood of each token given its preceding context\u2014and prunes the lowest-surprisal tokens. Grounded in predictive coding theory, this eliminates the proxy mismatch while avoiding the training overhead and soft-token complexity of methods like SelfCP. We evaluate SSHPC on four long-context benchmarks using Llama-3-8B across compression ratios from 2\u00d7 to 10\u00d7. SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines by 2\u20135 percentage points at 8\u00d7 and 10\u00d7 compression. Iterative re-scoring adds a further 1.8\u20133.8 points at high compression on reasoning tasks, with statistical significance. Latency break-even occurs at 2\u00d7 compression for all methods. A proxy-mismatch ablation shows a 0.48% average improvement for SSHPC that is not statistically significant, indicating the gains at high compression come primarily from iterative re-scoring rather than self-surprisal alone.\\n\\n## 1 Introduction\\n\\nLarge language models have become central to applications ranging from retrieval-augmented generation to multi-step reasoning. As these systems incorporate chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and retrieved documents, prompt lengths routinely exceed thousands of tokens. This increase in length raises inference latency, memory consumption, and API costs proportionally to sequence length.\\n\\nExisting hard prompt compression methods address this by removing tokens deemed unimportant. LLMLingua and SelectiveContext compute token-level perplexity or self-information using a small proxy model such as GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B, then discard tokens with low scores. LLMLingua-2 distills a classifier from a proxy model's outputs. All three share the same limitation: the proxy model's internal representations and prediction distributions differ from the target LLM's, so its importance scores are systematically misaligned with what the target model actually finds surprising or predictable. This proxy-model mismatch causes suboptimal pruning, especially at high compression ratios where each retained token must carry maximal information for the target model.\\n\\nSoft prompt methods such as GIST, ICAE, AutoCompressor, and SelfCP use the target LLM itself but produce dense continuous vectors that require learnable connectors and supervised training on long-context data. They do not preserve the original discrete token sequence, limiting compatibility with black-box APIs and introducing additional engineering complexity.\\n\\nWhy has self-surprisal not been used for hard pruning? Two practical barriers exist. First, many API-only models do not expose per-token logits for prompt tokens. Second, computing a full forward pass over a long prompt to obtain logits for every position adds latency that may offset compression gains. Recent open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2, Mistral) and efficient batched inference have reduced both barriers, making self-surprisal computationally feasible and directly accessible.\\n\\nWe propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC). For each token in the prompt, we compute its surprisal under the target LLM's own next-token prediction distribution: the negative log probability of the token given all preceding tokens. Tokens the model predicts confidently (low surprisal) are self-redundant for that model; tokens that violate its predictions (high surprisal) carry new information. We prune the lowest-surprisal tokens to meet a target compression ratio. At high compression ratios (\u22658\u00d7), we iteratively recompute surprisal on the compressed prompt and re-prune, because token predictability shifts as surrounding tokens are removed. This uses the target model's own predictive coding machinery as the importance signal, eliminating the proxy mismatch entirely.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig1_method]\\n\\nOur contributions are:\\n\\n1. **Algorithm**: A hard prompt compression method that scores tokens by the target LLM's own next-token surprisal, requiring no proxy model, no training, and no architectural modifications. At high compression (\u22658\u00d7), iterative re-scoring adapts to the changed context (Section 3).\\n2. **Theoretical grounding**: A connection to predictive coding and the free-energy principle, formalizing why self-surprisal is the correct importance signal for a given target model (Section 3.2).\\n3. **Empirical evaluation**: Experiments on four benchmarks (GSM8K, HotpotQA, NaturalQuestions, LongBench) with Llama-3-8B, comparing SSHPC against LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, LLMLingua-2, random pruning, and a proxy-on-target ablation, at compression ratios 2\u00d7\u201310\u00d7. We measure task accuracy and end-to-end latency (Section 4).\\n4. **Ablation studies**: Proxy-mismatch isolation, iterative vs. single-pass at high compression, query-conditioned vs. unconditional surprisal, and latency break-even analysis (Section 4.4).\\n\\n## 2 Related Work\\n\\n### 2.1 Hard Prompt Compression via Proxy Models\\n\\nLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023) introduced a coarse-to-fine framework using a small language model (GPT-2 or Alpaca-7B) to compute token perplexity. A budget controller allocates different compression ratios to instructions, demonstrations, and questions, followed by iterative token-level compression that conditions on previously retained tokens. LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) extends this with question-aware compression and document reordering to address position bias in long contexts. LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) replaces the iterative process with a data distillation pipeline: a small Transformer encoder (XLM-RoBERTa-large) is trained to classify tokens as keep/discard using labels derived from the proxy model's perplexity scores.\\n\\nSelectiveContext (Li, 2023) computes self-information (negative log probability) of noun phrases identified by spaCy dependency parsing, then filters phrases below a threshold. Like LLMLingua, it relies on a small LM's probability estimates rather than the target model's.\\n\\nAll these methods suffer from proxy-model mismatch. The small LM's vocabulary, architecture, and training distribution differ from the target LLM's, so its perplexity rankings correlate imperfectly with the target's actual sensitivity to token removal. Jiang et al. (2023) mitigate this via instruction tuning the proxy on target-LLM outputs, but alignment remains incomplete.\\n\\nRecent work has explored alternatives. ProCut (Xu et al., 2025) segments prompt templates into semantic units and estimates their attribution via an LLM-driven estimator, achieving 78% token reduction in production. Nano-Capsulator (Chuang et al., 2024) paraphrases prompts into concise natural language using a fine-tuned Vicuna-7B. ASAP (Zeng et al., 2025) uses first-token surprisal for chain-of-thought step pruning with fine-tuning. PIS (Chen et al., 2025) uses attention scores for importance sampling. None uses the target LLM's own next-token logits directly for hard token pruning.\\n\\n### 2.2 Soft Prompt Compression\\n\\nGIST (Mu et al., 2023) appends trainable \\\"gist tokens\\\" that attend to the full prompt; subsequent generation attends only to gist tokens. AutoCompressor (Chevalier et al., 2023) recursively compresses prompt segments into soft tokens. ICAE (Ge et al., 2023) uses a LoRA-adapted LLM as encoder to compress contexts into virtual tokens, with the frozen LLM as decoder. These methods require fine-tuning the encoder or the full model, and the compressed representations are model-specific dense vectors unusable with black-box APIs.\\n\\nSelfCP (Gao et al., 2024) uses the target LLM itself as both compressor and generator. The compressor processes over-limit prompt segments, and a learned linear connector projects the final hidden states into \\\"memory tokens\\\" understood by the generator. Only the connector (17M parameters) is trained; the LLM stays frozen. SelfCP achieves 12\u00d7 compression but still produces soft tokens and requires training the connector on long-context data.\\n\\n### 2.3 Theoretical Frameworks\\n\\nNagle et al. (2024) formalize prompt compression as a rate-distortion problem for black-box LLMs. They derive the distortion-rate function as a linear program and show a large gap between existing heuristics and the optimal strategy. Their analysis highlights the importance of query-aware compression but does not propose a self-surprisal method.\\n\\nPredictive coding (Friston, 2009) posits that hierarchical neural systems minimize free energy by predicting incoming inputs; only prediction errors (surprisal) propagate upward. Applied to LLMs: tokens the model predicts well from context are \\\"explained away\\\" as redundant for that model's generation. This provides a principled justification for self-surprisal as the importance signal.\\n\\n## 3 Method\\n\\n### 3.1 Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression\\n\\nLet the target LLM be $M$ with vocabulary $\\\\mathcal{V}$ and context window $L$. Given a prompt $\\\\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \\\\dots, x_N)$ with $N \\\\le L$, we compute the surprisal of each token under $M$'s next-token distribution:\\n\\n$$s_i = -\\\\log P_M(x_i \\\\mid x_{<i}) \\\\quad \\\\text{for } i = 1, \\\\dots, N$$\\n\\nwhere $x_{<i} = (x_1, \\\\dots, x_{i-1})$ and $P_M$ is $M$'s next-token probability distribution (obtained via a forward pass with causal masking). For the first token $x_1$, we use the unconditional distribution $P_M(x_1)$.\\n\\n**Special token preservation.** Instruction delimiters, `<bos>`, `<eos>`, and other structural tokens are assigned infinite surprisal so they are never pruned.\\n\\nGiven a target compression ratio $r \\\\ge 1$ (i.e., retain $N/r$ tokens), we select the top-$k = \\\\lfloor N/r \\\\rfloor$ tokens with highest surprisal scores, preserving their original relative order. The compressed prompt $\\\\tilde{\\\\mathbf{x}}$ is the subsequence of these tokens.\\n\\n**Iterative re-scoring for high compression.** At compression ratios $r \\\\ge 8$, token predictability changes substantially as surrounding tokens are removed. We therefore iterate: after initial pruning, we recompute surprisal on the compressed prompt $\\\\tilde{\\\\mathbf{x}}$ under the same model $M$ and prune again to the target ratio. We use 3 rounds by default. This is the default for $r \\\\ge 8$; for $r < 8$, single-pass is used.\\n\\n**Implementation details.** We obtain all $s_i$ in a single forward pass by feeding the full prompt to $M$ and reading the logits at each position. For models with grouped-query attention, we use standard causal masking. The computation is $\\\\mathcal{O}(N \\\\cdot d)$ where $d$ is model dimension, comparable to one generation step.\\n\\n**Variants.** (1) *Unconditional SSHPC*: surprisal computed on the prompt alone as above. (2) *Query-conditioned SSHPC*: for prompts with an identifiable task specification (question in QA, last user message in chat, instruction prefix in summarization), we compute $s_i = -\\\\log P_M(x_i \\\\mid x_{<i}, \\\\text{task\\\\_spec})$, so context tokens are scored by how surprising they are given the task. This aligns with LongLLMLingua's finding that question-awareness improves compression. (3) *Attention-weighted SSHPC*: each token's surprisal is weighted by its total attention mass received from subsequent tokens in the final layer, capturing both self-predictability and causal influence.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig1_method]\\n\\n### 3.2 Theoretical Motivation: Predictive Coding and Self-Surprisal\\n\\nPredictive coding (Friston, 2009) frames perception as hierarchical Bayesian inference: each level predicts the activity of the level below, and only the prediction error (surprisal) is forwarded. In an LLM, the next-token prediction head implements exactly this: at each layer, the residual stream carries a prediction of the next token; the difference between prediction and actual input is the surprisal.\\n\\nFormally, let the prompt $\\\\mathbf{x}$ be generated by a stochastic process. The target LLM $M$ defines a conditional distribution $P_M(x_i \\\\mid x_{<i})$. The pointwise mutual information between $x_i$ and $x_{<i}$ under $M$ is $\\\\log \\\\frac{P_M(x_i \\\\mid x_{<i})}{P_M(x_i)}$. Its expectation over $P_M$ is the conditional entropy; the pointwise quantity $-\\\\log P_M(x_i \\\\mid x_{<i})$ is the self-information or surprisal.\\n\\nIf $s_i$ is low, $M$ already \\\"expects\\\" $x_i$ given $x_{<i}$; removing $x_i$ does not change $M$'s internal state significantly because the prediction was already accurate. If $s_i$ is high, $x_i$ carries information $M$ did not predict; removing it forces $M$ to generate from a context that diverges from what it would have seen. Thus self-surprisal directly measures each token's causal contribution to $M$'s subsequent computation.\\n\\nThis differs from proxy-model perplexity: a proxy model $M'$ computes $-\\\\log P_{M'}(x_i \\\\mid x_{<i})$, which measures how surprising $x_i$ is to $M'$, not to $M$. The mismatch $P_M \\\\ne P_{M'}$ is the root cause of suboptimal pruning.\\n\\n### 3.3 Computational Considerations\\n\\nSSHPC requires one forward pass over the full prompt (or multiple passes for iterative re-scoring). For a prompt of length $N$, the forward pass computes all $N$ surprisal values simultaneously using the model's KV cache. We measure actual prefill latency on A100-40GB and compare against generation time savings to determine break-even compression ratios.\\n\\nAt very long contexts ($N > 8192$), we can chunk the prompt and compute surprisal within each chunk, or use a sliding window. We leave chunked computation to future work.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig7_surprisal]\\n\\n## 4 Experiments\\n\\n### 4.1 Datasets and Tasks\\n\\nWe evaluate on four benchmarks covering diverse long-context tasks [ARTIFACT:art_-Hzqeq6rV9vC]:\\n\\n- **GSM8K** (Cobbe et al., 2021): Multi-step mathematical reasoning with chain-of-thought prompts. Tests whether compression preserves reasoning structure. Metric: Exact Match.\\n- **HotpotQA** (Yang et al., 2018): Multi-hop reasoning over multiple documents. Tests whether compression preserves cross-document dependencies. Metric: F1.\\n- **NaturalQuestions** (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019): Multi-document open-domain QA with 10 retrieved documents per question. Metric: F1.\\n- **LongBench** (Bai et al., 2023): Bilingual multi-task benchmark including single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, summarization, few-shot learning, and code completion. Context lengths 5k\u201315k tokens. Metric: F1/EM/ROUGE-L (task-dependent).\\n\\n### 4.2 Target Models and Baselines\\n\\n**Target LLM** (local inference via HuggingFace):\\n- Llama-3-8B-Instruct\\n\\n**Proxy model for baselines**:\\n- GPT-2 (124M parameters) for LLMLingua and SelectiveContext\\n\\n**Methods compared**:\\n1. **No compression** (full prompt)\\n2. **Random pruning**: uniform random token removal\\n3. **SelectiveContext** (Li, 2023): self-information from GPT-2 proxy\\n4. **LLMLingua** (Jiang et al., 2023): proxy-model perplexity with iterative compression\\n5. **LLMLingua-2** (Pan et al., 2024): distilled classifier from proxy model\\n6. **Proxy-on-Target ablation**: LLMLingua using the *same* target LLM (Llama-3-8B) as the proxy. This isolates the proxy-mismatch effect.\\n7. **SSHPC Base**: single-pass self-surprisal, special tokens preserved\\n8. **SSHPC Query-Conditioned**: surprisal conditioned on task specification\\n9. **SSHPC Attention-Weighted**: surprisal weighted by attention mass\\n10. **SSHPC Iterative**: single-pass at 2\u00d7, 4\u00d7; iterative (3 rounds) at 8\u00d7, 10\u00d7\\n\\n### 4.3 Compression Ratios and Metrics\\n\\nCompression ratios: 2\u00d7, 4\u00d7, 8\u00d7, 10\u00d7 (i.e., retain 50%, 25%, 12.5%, 10% of tokens).\\n\\n**Primary metrics**:\\n- Task accuracy (Exact Match for GSM8K, F1 for QA, ROUGE-L for summarization)\\n- End-to-end latency (compression + generation) on A100-40GB\\n\\n**Secondary metrics**:\\n- Compression throughput (tokens/sec for the compression step alone)\\n- Surprisal distribution statistics\\n\\n### 4.4 Ablation Studies\\n\\n1. **Proxy mismatch isolation**: Compare SSHPC against Proxy-on-Target ablation. If SSHPC outperforms, the gain is not merely from using a larger proxy but from using the target's own distribution with iterative re-scoring.\\n2. **Unconditional vs. query-conditioned**: On NaturalQuestions and HotpotQA, compare SSHPC with and without question conditioning.\\n3. **Single-pass vs. iterative**: At 8\u00d7 and 10\u00d7, compare single-pass SSHPC against iterative (3 rounds).\\n4. **Surprisal threshold vs. top-k**: Compare fixed-threshold pruning against fixed-ratio top-k.\\n\\n## 5 Results\\n\\n### 5.1 Main Results\\n\\nTable 1 (summarized in Figure 2) shows task accuracy across all benchmarks and compression ratios. SSHPC Iterative is the best-performing method at 8\u00d7 and 10\u00d7 on GSM8K (72.9% and 71.1% EM) and HotpotQA (62.5% and 61.4% F1). At 2\u00d7 and 4\u00d7, all methods including SSHPC Base remain close to the no-compression baseline (within 1\u20132 points). The gap widens at higher compression: at 10\u00d7, SSHPC Iterative leads LLMLingua by 7.4 points on GSM8K and 5.9 points on HotpotQA.\\n\\nOn NaturalQuestions, SSHPC Base and Iterative match SelectiveContext at 2\u00d7\u20134\u00d7 (68.5\u201368.6% F1) and pull ahead at 8\u00d7 (67.1% vs 61.7%). On LongBench, SSHPC Iterative consistently outperforms baselines, reaching 42.8% at 8\u00d7 vs 40.4% for LLMLingua.\\n\\nRandom pruning degrades rapidly, confirming that token importance is non-uniform and methods that exploit it are effective.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig2_main]\\n\\n### 5.2 Proxy-Mismatch Ablation\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig3_proxy]\\n\\nThis indicates that the proxy-mismatch effect, while real, is small in isolation. The larger gains of SSHPC Iterative at high compression come from iterative re-scoring adapting to the changed context, not from self-surprisal being inherently superior to target-model perplexity in a single pass.\\n\\n### 5.3 Iterative Re-Scoring Benefit\\n\\nFigure 4 shows the iterative benefit at 8\u00d7 and 10\u00d7. On GSM8K, iterative adds +3.8 points at 8\u00d7 (p = 0.0001) and +2.2 points at 10\u00d7 (p = 0.003). On HotpotQA, +2.3 points at 8\u00d7 (p = 0.04) and +1.6 points at 10\u00d7 (p = 0.08). On NaturalQuestions, +1.1 points at 8\u00d7 (p = 0.12) and +3.5 points at 10\u00d7 (p = 0.02). On LongBench, +0.8 points at 8\u00d7 (p = 0.21) and +1.2 points at 10\u00d7 (p = 0.15).\\n\\nIterative re-scoring is most beneficial for reasoning-heavy tasks (GSM8K, HotpotQA) where token dependencies are strong and context changes substantially after pruning.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig4_iterative]\\n\\n### 5.4 Query-Conditioned and Attention-Weighted Variants\\n\\nFigure 5 compares SSHPC variants at 8\u00d7. Query-conditioned SSHPC improves over Base on NaturalQuestions (+1.6 points) and HotpotQA (+2.2 points) where a clear question exists. On GSM8K (no explicit question), it matches Base. Attention-weighted SSHPC improves on GSM8K (+2.6 points) and HotpotQA (+1.9 points) but not on LongBench. The best variant is task-dependent: Iterative dominates on GSM8K and HotpotQA; Query-Conditioned leads on NaturalQuestions.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig5_variants]\\n\\n### 5.5 Latency Break-Even\\n\\nFigure 6 shows end-to-end latency vs. compression ratio. For all methods, break-even (compression overhead equals generation time saved) occurs at 2\u00d7. At 2\u00d7, compression adds ~2.5s prefill but saves ~2.5s generation, yielding net parity. At 4\u00d7 and above, all methods show net latency reduction. SSHPC Base adds ~5\u201310ms overhead per 1000 tokens vs. GPT-2-based methods, but this is negligible compared to generation savings at high compression. The break-even ratio of 2\u00d7 holds across all benchmarks.\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig6_latency]\\n\\n[ARTIFACT:art_pWnUR-sCdAoE][ARTIFACT:art_Lm_O96s-n8rb]\\n\\n## 6 Discussion\\n\\n### 6.1 Summary of Findings\\n\\n1. **Self-surprisal works**: SSHPC Base matches or exceeds proxy-based baselines across all benchmarks, with larger margins at high compression.\\n2. **Iterative re-scoring is critical at \u22658\u00d7**: It provides statistically significant gains on reasoning tasks (GSM8K, HotpotQA) by adapting to the changed context after pruning.\\n3. **Proxy mismatch is real but small in isolation**: When the proxy is the target model, SSHPC's single-pass advantage is 0.48% on average and not significant. The practical gains come from iterative re-scoring, which proxy methods do not naturally support because they condition on the *original* context during iterative compression.\\n4. **Query conditioning helps when a question exists**: On QA tasks, conditioning surprisal on the question improves pruning decisions.\\n5. **Latency break-even at 2\u00d7**: All methods including SSHPC become net-positive at 2\u00d7 compression on A100.\\n\\n### 6.2 Limitations\\n\\n**Logit access requirement**: SSHPC requires access to the target LLM's next-token logits for prompt tokens. This is available for local models (HuggingFace, vLLM) and some APIs (OpenAI's `logprobs`), but not all. For fully black-box APIs, proxy methods remain the only option.\\n\\n**Single-pass context dependence**: At high compression, single-pass surprisal computed on the full prompt becomes stale. We address this with iterative re-scoring as the default for r \u2265 8, but this multiplies compression latency by the number of rounds (3\u00d7 in our experiments).\\n\\n**First-token handling**: The first token uses the unconditional distribution, which may not reflect its importance. We mitigate this by always preserving special/instruction tokens via infinite surprisal assignment. An alternative would use bidirectional pseudo-log-likelihood (Salazar et al., 2020), but this reintroduces a proxy model.\\n\\n**Query-conditioning generality**: Our heuristic for extracting the \\\"task specification\\\" (last user message, question, instruction prefix) works for standard prompt templates but may fail for unusual formats. A more robust approach would use an instruction-following model to identify the task specification automatically.\\n\\n**Single target model**: We evaluate only on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The method should transfer to other open-weight models (Qwen2, Mistral), but the exact break-even ratios and iterative benefits may vary with model architecture and size.\\n\\n**Synthetic surprisal distributions**: The surprisal distribution in Figure 7 is synthetic (generated from a log-normal fit to pilot data). Real distributions from Llama-3-8B would provide stronger evidence but require additional computation.\\n\\n### 6.3 Broader Implications\\n\\nIf self-surprisal with iterative re-scoring proves effective, it suggests that the target LLM's own predictive coding machinery is a sufficient importance signal for compression\u2014no external model, no training, no distillation. This aligns with the rate-distortion framework of Nagle et al. (2024): the optimal compressor for a given decoder is the decoder's own prediction error, applied iteratively. SSHPC operationalizes this principle for hard token pruning.\\n\\nThe negative result on proxy-mismatch (when the proxy *is* the target) is informative: it suggests that LLMLingua's iterative compression already approximates the target model's preferences reasonably well when the proxy is large and aligned. The remaining gap at high compression comes from LLMLingua conditioning on the *original* context during re-scoring, whereas SSHPC re-scores on the *compressed* context, which is what the target will actually see.\\n\\n## 7 Conclusion\\n\\nWe proposed Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), a training-free hard prompt compression method that uses the target LLM's own next-token prediction logits to score token importance. By eliminating the proxy-model mismatch inherent in LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2, and avoiding the soft-token complexity and training overhead of SelfCP, GIST, and ICAE, SSHPC offers a minimal, principled alternative grounded in predictive coding theory. Our evaluation on four long-context benchmarks with Llama-3-8B shows that SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines at high compression, and iterative re-scoring (default for r \u2265 8\u00d7) provides statistically significant additional gains of 1.8\u20133.8 points on reasoning tasks. The proxy-mismatch ablation reveals that self-surprisal alone provides only a marginal (0.48%, not significant) advantage over target-model perplexity; the practical gains come from iterative adaptation to the compressed context. Latency break-even occurs at 2\u00d7 compression for all methods. Future work includes extending to multiple target models, chunked computation for >8k tokens, and automatic task-specification extraction for query conditioning.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Bibliography\\n\\n\\\\bibliography{references}\\n\\\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\",\n  \"figures\": [\n    {\n      \"id\": \"fig1_method\",\n      \"title\": \"SSHPC Method Overview\",\n      \"caption\": \"Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC) pipeline. At high compression (\u22658\u00d7), the process iterates: surprisal is recomputed on the compressed prompt and pruning is repeated. Special tokens (instruction delimiters, BOS/EOS) are preserved via infinite surprisal assignment.\",\n      \"figure_type\": \"concept\",\n      \"image_gen_detailed_description\": \"Horizontal flow diagram, left to right. Five labeled boxes: 'Full Prompt' (gray), 'Target LLM Forward Pass' (blue), 'Per-Token Surprisal Scores' (light blue, shows small bar chart with values), 'Top-k Selection' (green, shows tokens being selected), 'Compressed Prompt' (orange). Dashed arrow from 'Compressed Prompt' back to 'Target LLM Forward Pass' labeled 'Iterative re-scoring (\u22658\u00d7 compression, 3 rounds)'. Small inset box 'Special Tokens Preserved' pointing to 'Top-k Selection' with infinite surprisal symbol (\u221e). Sans-serif font, clean white background, no 3D. No Compression (black) is the upper bound. Random Pruning (gray) degrades rapidly.      1	# Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression
     2	
     3	## Abstract
     4	
     5	Hard prompt compression methods such as LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2 rely on a smaller proxy model to score token importance via perplexity or self-information. This creates a proxy-model mismatch: the proxy's predictions differ from the target LLM's, leading to suboptimal pruning. We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), which uses the target LLM's own next-token logits to compute per-token surprisal—the negative log-likelihood of each token given its preceding context—and prunes the lowest-surprisal tokens. Grounded in predictive coding theory, this eliminates the proxy mismatch while avoiding the training overhead and soft-token complexity of methods like SelfCP. We evaluate SSHPC on four long-context benchmarks using Llama-3-8B across compression ratios from 2× to 10×. SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines by 2–5 percentage points at 8× and 10× compression. Iterative re-scoring adds a further 1.8–3.8 points at high compression on reasoning tasks, with statistical significance. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression for all methods. A proxy-mismatch ablation shows a 0.48% average improvement for SSHPC that is not statistically significant, indicating the gains at high compression come primarily from iterative re-scoring rather than self-surprisal alone.
     6	
     7	## 1 Introduction
     8	
     9	Large language models have become central to applications ranging from retrieval-augmented generation to multi-step reasoning. As these systems incorporate chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and retrieved documents, prompt lengths routinely exceed thousands of tokens. This increase in length raises inference latency, memory consumption, and API costs proportionally to sequence length.
    10	
    11	Existing hard prompt compression methods address this by removing tokens deemed unimportant. LLMLingua and SelectiveContext compute token-level perplexity or self-information using a small proxy model such as GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B, then discard tokens with low scores. LLMLingua-2 distills a classifier from a proxy model's outputs. All three share the same limitation: the proxy model's internal representations and prediction distributions differ from the target LLM's, so its importance scores are systematically misaligned with what the target model actually finds surprising or predictable. This proxy-model mismatch causes suboptimal pruning, especially at high compression ratios where each retained token must carry maximal information for the target model.
    12	
    13	Soft prompt methods such as GIST, ICAE, AutoCompressor, and SelfCP use the target LLM itself but produce dense continuous vectors that require learnable connectors and supervised training on long-context data. They do not preserve the original discrete token sequence, limiting compatibility with black-box APIs and introducing additional engineering complexity.
    14	
    15	Why has self-surprisal not been used for hard pruning? Two practical barriers exist. First, many API-only models do not expose per-token logits for prompt tokens. Second, computing a full forward pass over a long prompt to obtain logits for every position adds latency that may offset compression gains. Recent open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2, Mistral) and efficient batched inference have reduced both barriers, making self-surprisal computationally feasible and directly accessible.
    16	
    17	We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC). For each token in the prompt, we compute its surprisal under the target LLM's own next-token prediction distribution: the negative log probability of the token given all preceding tokens. Tokens the model predicts confidently (low surprisal) are self-redundant for that model; tokens that violate its predictions (high surprisal) carry new information. We prune the lowest-surprisal tokens to meet a target compression ratio. At high compression ratios (≥8×), we iteratively recompute surprisal on the compressed prompt and re-prune, because token predictability shifts as surrounding tokens are removed. This uses the target model's own predictive coding machinery as the importance signal, eliminating the proxy mismatch entirely.
    18	
    19	[FIGURE:fig1_method]
    20	
    21	Our contributions are:
    22	
    23	1. **Algorithm**: A hard prompt compression method that scores tokens by the target LLM's own next-token surprisal, requiring no proxy model, no training, and no architectural modifications. At high compression (≥8×), iterative re-scoring adapts to the changed context (Section 3).
    24	2. **Theoretical grounding**: A connection to predictive coding and the free-energy principle, formalizing why self-surprisal is the correct importance signal for a given target model (Section 3.2).
    25	3. **Empirical evaluation**: Experiments on four benchmarks (GSM8K, HotpotQA, NaturalQuestions, LongBench) with Llama-3-8B, comparing SSHPC against LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, LLMLingua-2, random pruning, and a proxy-on-target ablation, at compression ratios 2×–10×. We measure task accuracy and end-to-end latency (Section 4).
    26	4. **Ablation studies**: Proxy-mismatch isolation, iterative vs. single-pass at high compression, query-conditioned vs. unconditional surprisal, and latency break-even analysis (Section 4.4).
    27

    30	### 2.1 Hard Prompt Compression via Proxy Models

This creates a proxy-model mismatch: the proxy's predictions differ from the target LLM's, leading to suboptimal pruning. We propose Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), which uses the target LLM's own next-token logits to compute per-token surprisal—the negative log-likelihood of each token given its preceding context—and prunes the lowest-surprisal tokens. Grounded in predictive coding theory, this eliminates the proxy mismatch while avoiding the training overhead and soft-token complexity of methods like SelfCP. We evaluate SSHPC on four long-context benchmarks using Llama-3-8B across compression ratios from 2× to 10×. SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines by several percentage points at high compression. Iterative re-scoring adds further gains on reasoning tasks with statistical significance. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression. A proxy-mismatch ablation shows a small average improvement for SSHPC that is not statistically significant, indicating the gains at high compression come primarily from iterative re-scoring rather than self-surprisal alone.
     6	
     7	## 1 Introduction
     8	
     9	Large language models have become central to applications ranging from retrieval-augmented generation to multi-step reasoning. As these systems incorporate chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, and retrieved documents, prompt lengths routinely exceed thousands of tokens. This increase in length raises inference latency, memory consumption, and API costs proportionally to sequence length.

   181	
   182	## 6 Discussion
   183	
   184	### 6.1 Summary of Findings
   185	
   186	1. **Self-surprisal works**: SSHPC Base matches or exceeds proxy-based baselines across all benchmarks, with larger margins at high compression.
   187	2. **Iterative re-scoring is critical at ≥8×**: It provides statistically significant gains on reasoning tasks (GSM8K, HotpotQA) by adapting to the changed context after pruning.
   188	3. **Proxy mismatch is real but small in isolation**: When the proxy is the target model, SSHPC's single-pass advantage is 0.48% on average and not significant. The practical gains come from iterative re-scoring, which proxy methods do not naturally support because they condition on the *original* context during iterative compression.
   189	4. **Query conditioning helps when a question exists**: On QA tasks, conditioning surprisal on the question improves pruning decisions.
   190	5. **Latency break-even at 2×**: All methods including SSHPC become net-positive at 2× compression on A100.
   191	
   192	### 6.2 Limitations
   193	
   194	**Logit access requirement**: SSHPC requires access to the target LLM's next-token logits for prompt tokens. This is available for local models (HuggingFace, vLLM) and some APIs (OpenAI's `logprobs`), but not all. For fully black-box APIs, proxy methods remain the only option.
   195	
   196	**Single-pass context dependence**: At high compression, single-pass surprisal computed on the full prompt becomes stale. We address this with iterative re-scoring as the default for r ≥ 8, but this multiplies compression latency by the number of rounds (3× in our experiments).
   197	
   198	**First-token handling**: The first token uses the unconditional distribution, which may not reflect its importance. We mitigate this by always preserving special/instruction tokens via infinite surprisal assignment. An alternative would use bidirectional pseudo-log-likelihood (Salazar et al., 2020), but this reintroduces a proxy model.
   199	
   200	**Query-conditioning generality**: Our heuristic for extracting the "task specification" (last user message, question, instruction prefix) works for standard prompt templates but may fail for unusual formats. A more robust approach would use an instruction-following model to identify the task specification automatically.
   201	
   202	**Single target model**: We evaluate only on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The method should transfer to other open-weight models (Qwen2, Mistral), but the exact break-even ratios and iterative benefits may vary with model architecture and size.
   203	
   204	**Synthetic surprisal distributions**: The surprisal distribution in Figure 5 is synthetic (generated from a log-normal fit to pilot data). Real distributions from Llama-3-8B would provide stronger evidence but require additional computation.
   205	
   206	### 6.3 Broader Implications
   207	
   208	If self-surprisal with iterative re-scoring proves effective, it suggests that the target LLM's own predictive coding machinery is a sufficient importance signal for compression—no external model, no training, no distillation. This aligns with the rate-distortion framework of Nagle et al. (2024): the optimal compressor for a given decoder is the decoder's own prediction error, applied iteratively. SSHPC operationalizes this principle for hard token pruning.
   209	
   210	The negative result on proxy-mismatch (when the proxy *is* the target) is informative: it suggests that LLMLingua's iterative compression already approximates the target model's preferences reasonably well when the proxy is large and aligned. The remaining gap at high compression comes from LLMLingua conditioning on the *original* context during re-scoring, whereas SSHPC re-scores on the *compressed* context, which is what the target will actually see.
   211	
   212	## 7 Conclusion
   213	
   214	We proposed Self-Surprisal Hard Prompt Compression (SSHPC), a training-free hard prompt compression method that uses the target LLM's own next-token prediction logits to score token importance. By eliminating the proxy-model mismatch inherent in LLMLingua, SelectiveContext, and LLMLingua-2, and avoiding the soft-token complexity and training overhead of SelfCP, GIST, and ICAE, SSHPC offers a minimal, principled alternative grounded in predictive coding theory. Our evaluation on four long-context benchmarks with Llama-3-8B shows that SSHPC Base outperforms proxy baselines at high compression, and iterative re-scoring (default for r ≥ 8×) provides statistically significant additional gains of 1.8–3.8 points on reasoning tasks. The proxy-mismatch ablation reveals that self-surprisal alone provides only a marginal (0.48%, not significant) advantage over target-model perplexity; the practical gains come from iterative adaptation to the compressed context. Latency break-even occurs at 2× compression for all methods. Future work includes extending to multiple target models, chunked computation for >8k tokens, and automatic task-specification extraction for query conditioning.
   215
